debrief.title: Customers
text: Tell affected customers which invoice is valid and that duplicates won't be charged twice.
Check with billing that no duplicate was collected.

debrief.title: Month-end planning
text: Month end is a known peak: load test the whole invoicing path, including the tax API, before it.
Agree response-time expectations with the tax API's owner.

sayIt.question: A known peak period exposed a weakness in a dependency. How do you plan for peaks?
points: Identify the peaks in the calendar.
Load test the full path, including third-party dependencies.
Agree performance expectations with dependency owners.
Make duplicate-safe behaviour a requirement.
Review after each peak and feed back into planning.

tasks: How do you stabilise the service today?
What goes into the operational readiness checklist?

debrief.title: Stabilising today
text: Deploy a smaller max.poll.records so each batch finishes inside the interval; watch rebalances stop.
Pause invoice emails until the duplicate check is in, then resume.

debrief.title: Readiness checklist
text: For each consumer: worst-case processing time per batch versus max.poll.interval.ms.
An alert on rebalance frequency and on CommitFailedException in logs.

sayIt.question: How would you get a consumer group out of a rebalance loop during an incident?
points: Recognise the signs: repeated rebalances, CommitFailedException, growing lag.
Find the slow step and compare batch time to max.poll.interval.ms.
Shrink the batch or extend the interval to stop the loop.
Contain side effects while it settles.
Add monitoring and a checklist item so it is caught earlier.

tasks: Which settings do you change, and to what?
How do you make the email idempotent?

debrief.title: Settings
text: Work out the budget: at 900 ms per record, 50 records is 45 seconds, well inside 5 minutes. Set max.poll.records=50.
Consider group.protocol=consumer for faster, incremental rebalances; it is the newer protocol, opt-in on the client since Kafka 4.0.
Use static membership (group.instance.id) as well, so rolling deployments don't trigger rebalances.

debrief.title: Idempotent emails
text: Store the invoice ID when an email is sent, and check it first. A redelivered event then finds the record and skips the send.

sayIt.question: Explain session.timeout.ms versus max.poll.interval.ms, and what causes a rebalance storm.
points: Heartbeats and the session timeout detect a dead process.
max.poll.interval.ms detects a live process that stopped making progress.
A batch that takes longer than the interval gets the consumer removed, and the group rebalances.
Fix by sizing max.poll.records to the slowest processing, or raising the interval.
Make effects idempotent, because rebalances redeliver; use static membership and the newer protocol to reduce rebalances.

scenarios.title: The lag that wouldn't drop
scenarios.outcome: Lag kept growing, the team doubled the consumers, six of them sat idle, and the database got slower.

content.bookmark: In a consumer group each partition has one owner, so the partition count caps how many consumers can work. Find what is slow before adding consumers.

check.prompt: A topic has 6 partitions and a group has 12 consumers. How many consumers receive records?
check.why: Each partition is consumed by exactly one member of a group at a time, so at most 6 members have work.

check.prompt: In kafka-consumer-groups --describe, what is LAG?
options: The time since the last record
The log-end offset minus the group's committed offset for that partition
The number of consumers in the group
check.why: The tool shows CURRENT-OFFSET (committed), LOG-END-OFFSET and LAG, the difference, per partition.

check.prompt: Lag grows on every partition evenly, and each consumer is busy waiting on database writes. What helps most?
options: Making each consumer's processing faster, for example by batching the database writes
check.why: The bottleneck is the work per record. Extra consumers past the partition count idle; below it, they add load to the same slow database.

check.prompt: Which Kafka 4.2+ feature lets more consumers than partitions share the work?
options: Share groups, which acknowledge records one by one and give up per-partition ordering
check.why: In a share group, consumers share partitions cooperatively, so there can be more consumers than partitions. The cost is ordering within a partition.

caseStudy.setting: A ride-hailing company (fictional) streams trip-completed events to a trips topic with 6 partitions. A billing consumer group of 6 instances reads each trip and writes a fare row to a relational database, one insert per trip.

events.what: Evening demand doubles. Lag on trips climbs steadily on all six partitions.
The on-call engineer scales the billing group from 6 to 12 instances. Lag keeps climbing.
The database team reports connection pressure and slower inserts. Six of the new instances show no assigned partitions.

pipeline: trips topic · 6 partitions
Billing group · scaled from 6 to 12 instances
Each record · one INSERT into the fares database
Commit · after each poll's records are written
tasks: Why didn't doubling the consumers help?
What would actually bring the lag down?

debrief.title: Why more consumers didn't help
text: With 6 partitions, at most 6 members of a group can be assigned work. The 6 new instances joined, triggered a rebalance, and received nothing.

The real limit was the database: each consumer spent most of its time waiting for single-row inserts. The new instances that did get partitions after the rebalance only added connections to the same database.

debrief.title: What brings lag down
text: Make each consumer faster: write a poll's records to the database in one batch, instead of one insert per record.
If one consumer per partition is truly at its limit, more partitions raise the ceiling, sized with headroom and planned, because adding them moves keys (scenario 4).
If per-partition order doesn't matter for this work, a share group (production-ready since 4.2) allows more consumers than partitions.

debrief.title: Reading lag correctly
text: Lag that grows evenly on all partitions points to slow processing or too little parallelism. Lag on one partition only points to a hot key (scenario 8) or a stuck record (scenario 9).
The consumer's own records-lag-max metric is based on its current position, not the committed offset, so it can differ from the tool's LAG column.

takeaway: The partition count caps a group's parallelism.
Find the slow step before adding consumers.
Even lag says slow work; lag on one partition says a hot key or a stuck record.
content.honesty: If you haven't tuned a lagging consumer, say so and explain how you'd diagnose it. If you have, lead with what the bottleneck turned out to be.

tasks: What questions would you ask before approving more instances?
What should the team commit to measuring?

debrief.title: Questions
text: "Is lag the same on every partition or concentrated on one?" That separates slow work from a hot key.
"What is each consumer waiting on?" That finds the bottleneck.

debrief.title: Measures
text: Time from trip end to fare recorded, with a target.
Throughput per consumer before and after any change.

sayIt.question: Billing fell behind during a peak. How would you work with the team to fix it?
points: Ask for the shape of the lag before any fix.
Ask what the slow step is.
Know the ceiling: more consumers than partitions do nothing.
Agree a measurable target, like time from trip to fare.
Prefer the fix that addresses the bottleneck over adding capacity.

debrief.title: Impact
text: Fares recorded late may delay receipts and driver payouts. Check whether either was affected and tell drivers if payouts slip.

debrief.title: Planning
text: Agree peak volumes with the business, test billing at twice that, and size partitions and database capacity together.

sayIt.question: How would you plan capacity for a known demand peak?
points: Get peak volumes from the business, with growth.

Size Kafka partitions and downstream capacity together.
Watch time-to-processed as the customer-facing measure.
Review after the peak.

tasks: What do you do during the incident?
What goes in the runbook?

debrief.title: During the incident
text: Scale back to 6 instances to stop pointless rebalances and database load.
Agree with the database team whether a quick batching change or more database capacity is faster tonight.

debrief.title: Runbook
text: Check lag per partition first. Never scale a group beyond its partition count. Check downstream latency before scaling up.

sayIt.question: A consumer group is falling behind. Walk me through your first steps.
points: Look at lag per partition: even, or on one?
Check consumers' processing time and what they wait on.
Know that consumers beyond the partition count idle.
Coordinate with downstream owners before adding load.
Record the steps in a runbook.

tasks: How do you speed up the consumer?
When would you add partitions or use a share group?

debrief.title: Speeding it up
text: Batch the inserts per poll, inside one database transaction, and commit offsets after it succeeds.
Tune max.poll.records with the batch size, keeping each poll's work inside max.poll.interval.ms.

debrief.title: Partitions or a share group
text: More partitions if one consumer per partition is at its limit and order per trip still matters; plan it.
A share group if order doesn't matter and you want to scale consumers freely; records are acknowledged one by one.

sayIt.question: How do you scale Kafka consumption, and what limits it?
points: Parallelism within a group is capped by the partition count.
Diagnose before scaling: lag shape, processing time, downstream latency.
Make each consumer efficient: batch downstream writes.
Add partitions with headroom when the per-partition ceiling is reached, knowing keys move.
Share groups (4.2+) allow more consumers than partitions at the cost of ordering.

scenarios.title: The flash sale on one partition
scenarios.outcome: One seller's flash sale, keyed by seller ID, put 80% of the traffic on one partition, and more partitions changed nothing.

content.bookmark: A key always hashes to one partition. If one key carries most of the traffic, one partition and one consumer carry it, however many partitions there are.

check.prompt: Lag is high on one partition and near zero on the others. What is the likely cause?
options: Too few consumers in the group
A skewed key: one key sends far more records than the rest
check.why: Lag on one partition only, with one consumer saturated and the rest idle, is the classic sign of a hot key.

check.prompt: The topic is keyed by seller ID and one seller is hot. You double the partitions. What happens to that seller's records?
options: They still all go to one partition
check.why: The same key hashes to one partition whatever the count. More partitions add room for other keys, not for this one.

check.prompt: You change the key to seller ID plus a bucket number 0 to 3. What do you give up?
options: Ordering across that seller's records: order holds only within each bucket
check.why: Bucketing spreads the seller over up to four partitions. Order now holds within each bucket, not across all of the seller's records.

check.prompt: What does the producer do with a record that has no key?
options: Sends it to a sticky partition that changes after about a batch, spreading load
check.why: With no key the built-in partitioner sticks to a partition until at least batch.size bytes have gone, then moves on, which spreads load well. It gives no per-entity order.

caseStudy.setting: An online marketplace (fictional) publishes order events to marketplace.orders, keyed by seller ID, so each seller's orders are processed in order. A fulfilment group of 12 consumers reads 12 partitions and books couriers.

events.what: One large seller starts a flash sale. Within minutes, about 80% of all orders are theirs.
Lag on partition 7 climbs into the tens of thousands. The other 11 partitions are near zero. Couriers for the sale's orders are booked hours late.
The team raises the topic to 24 partitions and adds consumers. Partition 7's backlog doesn't move.

pipeline: Order service · key = seller ID
marketplace.orders · 12 partitions, raised to 24
Fulfilment group · one consumer per partition, books a courier per order
Courier API · called once per order
tasks: Why did adding partitions not help?
Does anything really need all of one seller's orders in order?

debrief.title: Why more partitions didn't help
text: Every record with that seller's ID hashes to the same partition, so one partition, and the single consumer that owns it, received 80% of the traffic.
Adding partitions gave other keys more room. The hot key stayed on one partition, and the change also moved other sellers' keys (scenario 4).

debrief.title: Choosing the key from what needs order
text: Booking a courier needs each order's own events in order, not every order of one seller. Keying by order ID spreads the sale evenly and keeps what matters in order.
Ask of any key: what is the smallest thing whose events must be applied in sequence? That is the key.

debrief.title: If the key really must stay
text: Bucket it: seller ID plus a bucket number. Load spreads over several partitions, and order holds only within each bucket.
Or route the known heavy seller to its own topic with its own consumers.
Watch for skew before it bites: per-partition bytes in, and lag per partition, not just total lag.

takeaway: One key, one partition, one consumer.
Key by the smallest thing that needs order.
More partitions can't split a hot key.

scenarios.title: One bad record
scenarios.outcome: A line of plain text in a JSON topic stopped a partition for six hours while the consumer crashed and restarted on it.

content.bookmark: A record that can never be processed must be moved aside to a dead-letter topic, with its details, so the partition behind it can move on.

check.prompt: A plain Java consumer meets a record its deserializer can't read. What happens?
options: poll throws RecordDeserializationException, and the consumer won't move past the record by itself
check.why: The exception carries the partition and offset. The application decides what to do: log it, send it to a dead-letter topic, and seek past it.

check.prompt: Does the Apache Kafka consumer client have a built-in dead-letter topic?
options: No; the application writes to a dead-letter topic itself
Yes, it is on by default
check.why: Kafka Connect (for sink connectors) and Kafka Streams have dead-letter settings. A plain consumer has none: you build it.

check.prompt: What does Kafka Streams do with a record it can't deserialize, by default?
options: Logs it and fails, stopping the application
Sends it to a dead-letter topic
check.why: The default handler is LogAndFailExceptionHandler. LogAndContinue skips, and errors.dead.letter.queue.topic.name sends records to a dead-letter topic.

check.prompt: What stops bad records from being written in the first place?
options: Producers serializing with a schema, checked by a schema registry
check.why: Schemaless JSON enforces nothing, so any text can be written. A schema-based serializer refuses data that doesn't fit before it reaches the topic.

caseStudy.setting: A bank (fictional) streams card transactions as JSON to card.transactions. A fraud-scoring consumer reads them and flags suspicious ones within seconds. A support engineer occasionally sends test messages using the console producer.

events.what: A support engineer testing connectivity sends the text "hello test" to card.transactions with the console producer.
The fraud consumer that owns that partition crashes on the record, restarts from its committed offset, reads the same record, and crashes again, about once a minute for six hours.
A customer reports fraud on their card that was never flagged. Every transaction on that partition since 02:10 was unscored.

pipeline: Card systems · produce JSON transactions, no schema
card.transactions · 24 partitions
Fraud consumer · JSON deserializer, crashes on any parse error
Platform · restarts the consumer automatically
tasks: Why did one record stop a whole partition?
What should the consumer do with a record it can never process?

debrief.title: Why one record stopped a partition
text: A partition is read in order. The consumer can't skip a record by itself: it either processes it or the application moves past it deliberately.
The consumer crashed before committing, so each restart resumed at the same offset and met the same record. Every record behind it on that partition waited for six hours.
This is a poison record: retrying can never help, because the record itself is the problem.

debrief.title: Moving it aside
text: Catch the deserialization error. Write the raw bytes, with the topic, partition, offset and error, to a dead-letter topic. Then seek past the record and carry on.
Alert on anything arriving in the dead-letter topic, and give it an owner who inspects and, if right, replays.
Separate permanent failures (bad data: dead-letter now) from transient ones (a timeout: retry later, scenario 10).

debrief.title: Stopping it at the source
text: Producers serializing with a schema (Avro or Protobuf with a schema registry) can't write arbitrary text.
Restrict who may write to production topics with ACLs, so test messages go to test topics.

takeaway: A poison record never succeeds on retry.
Dead-letter it with its context and move on, then alert.
Schemas and ACLs keep bad records out.
content.honesty: If you haven't handled poison records, say so and explain the pattern. If you have, say how you found the record and what you changed.

tasks: What questions would you ask?
What requirements would you add?

debrief.title: Questions
text: "What happens to all the other transactions when one is unreadable?"
"Who can write to the production topic?"

debrief.title: Requirements
text: One unreadable record never stops scoring for others; it is set aside and alerted within minutes.
Only the card systems can write transactions to production.

sayIt.question: How would you make sure one bad message can't stop a critical stream?
points: Name the risk: an unreadable message blocks everything behind it.

Require an alert and an owner for set-aside messages.
Require schemas so bad data is refused at the source.
Require write access only for the real producers.

tasks: What is the impact on customers?

debrief.title: Customers

debrief.title: Risk
text: Six hours of transactions unscored on one partition: report the window, the count and the fix to the risk owner.

sayIt.question: A control like fraud scoring silently stopped for part of the traffic. How do you handle it?
points: Scope the gap: which transactions, which hours.
Rescore and act on what was missed.
Report honestly to the risk owner.
Add monitoring of the control's coverage, not just its health.
Fund the prevention.

tasks: How do you run the incident?

debrief.title: Running it
text: Move the consumer past the record (seek or a reset of that partition's offset by one), rescore the backlog, then deploy the dead-letter handling.

debrief.title: Access and process
text: No test messages on production topics; a test topic and ACLs that enforce it.
An alert for repeated consumer restarts.

sayIt.question: A consumer is crash-looping on one message. What do you do?
points: Find the partition and offset from the error.
Unblock: move past the record deliberately, keeping a copy.
Process the backlog behind it.
Add dead-letter handling and an alert.
Close the gap that let the bad record in.

tasks: How do you implement the dead-letter path?
How would it differ in Connect or Streams?

debrief.title: In a plain consumer
text: Catch RecordDeserializationException, read its partition and offset, produce the raw bytes and error details to card.transactions.dlq, seek to offset plus one, continue.
Commit after the dead-letter write succeeds, so a crash doesn't lose the bad record.

debrief.title: In Connect and Streams
text: Connect sink connectors: errors.tolerance=all with errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name and context headers.
Streams: errors.dead.letter.queue.topic.name with the default handlers, or LogAndContinue to skip.

sayIt.question: How do you handle poison records in Kafka?
points: A poison record fails every time; retrying blocks the partition.
Plain consumer: catch the deserialization error, write it with context to a dead-letter topic, seek past.
Connect and Streams have dead-letter settings; the plain client doesn't.
Alert on and own the dead-letter topic.
Prevent with schemas and write ACLs.

scenarios.title: The retry storm
scenarios.outcome: A payment provider went down for 40 minutes, every layer retried at once, and the outage lasted three hours.

content.bookmark: When a dependency is down, retrying immediately and everywhere makes it worse. Back off with jitter, retry out of the main path, and stop calling when it is clearly down.

check.prompt: A consumer retries a failed call in place, inside its poll loop, for 10 minutes. What else happens?
options: Every record behind it on that partition waits, and the consumer can miss max.poll.interval.ms and be removed from its group
Kafka retries the call for you
check.why: A blocking retry holds up its partition, and if poll isn't called within max.poll.interval.ms (5 minutes by default) the group rebalances.

check.prompt: Four layers each make 3 attempts at a failing call. How many calls can reach the bottom layer for one request?
check.why: Retries multiply: 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81. Retry in one place, not every layer.

check.prompt: Why does the Kafka producer add random jitter to its retry backoff?
options: So many clients don't retry at the same moment
check.why: retry.backoff.ms grows exponentially to retry.backoff.max.ms with ±20% jitter, so clients don't retry in sync. The same idea applies to your own retries.

check.prompt: Retry topics move a failed record to a delayed topic and process it later. What do you lose?
options: Order: later records for the same key may be processed before the retried one
check.why: The main topic keeps flowing, so a retried record is processed after others with its key. Fine for independent events; dangerous where order matters.

caseStudy.setting: An e-commerce company (fictional) has a payment consumer that reads OrderPlaced events and calls an external payment provider. The call goes through an API gateway, an internal payment service and an HTTP client library, each with its own retry policy of 3 attempts, and the consumer itself retries 3 times in its poll loop.

events.what: The payment provider has a partial outage and starts timing out.
Calls to the provider jump to dozens of times normal volume. The provider starts rate-limiting the company entirely. Consumers block in retries, miss the poll interval and rebalance repeatedly.
The provider recovered at 10:40, but the company's payments only resumed at 13:00, after engineers stopped the consumers and restarted them slowly.

pipeline: Payment consumer · retries 3 times in the poll loop
HTTP client · retries 3 times
Internal payment service · retries 3 times
API gateway · retries 3 times, then the provider
tasks: Why did a 40-minute outage become a three-hour one?
Where should retries live in this design?

debrief.title: How the storm grew
text: Four layers of 3 attempts multiply: up to 81 calls to the provider for one order. Every consumer did this at once, immediately, with no backoff.
The flood made the provider rate-limit the company, so even after it recovered, calls kept failing and being retried.
Retrying in the poll loop held up whole partitions and pushed consumers past max.poll.interval.ms, so the group kept rebalancing and redelivering.

debrief.title: Where retries belong
text: Retry in one layer only, with exponential backoff and jitter, and a total time limit.
Move a record that keeps failing out of the main path: a retry topic with a delay (for example 1 minute, then 10, then an hour), then a dead-letter topic.
Put a circuit breaker in front of the provider: after a run of failures, stop calling for a while and pause the consumer instead of hammering a dependency that is down.

debrief.title: What Kafka gives you, and what it doesn't
text: The Kafka producer's own retries already use exponential backoff with jitter. Your calls to other systems don't, unless you build it.
A consumer can pause its partitions and keep calling poll, so it stays in the group while a dependency recovers.

takeaway: Retries multiply across layers.
Back off with jitter, retry in one place, and stop when it's down.
Move failing records out of the main path; know what order you give up.
content.honesty: If you haven't lived through a retry storm, say so and explain the arithmetic and the patterns. If you have, lead with how it was finally stopped.

tasks: What questions would you ask?

debrief.title: Questions
text: "How many layers retry a payment call, and how many times each?"
"When the provider is down, what happens to orders?"

debrief.title: Specified behaviour
text: During a provider outage, orders are held and paid when it recovers, within an agreed time; customers see an honest status.
Our calls to the provider never exceed an agreed rate, even during failures.

sayIt.question: A third-party service your product depends on goes down. What should the product do?
points: Degrade gracefully: hold work, show honest status.
Never make the outage worse with uncontrolled retries.
Recover automatically when it returns, within a target time.
Agree limits and expectations with the third party.
Test the outage before it happens.

tasks: What do you tell customers during the outage?

debrief.title: During
text: Tell customers orders are received and payment is delayed, rather than failing them.

debrief.title: After
text: Agree rate limits and outage communication with the provider, and consider a second provider for resilience.

sayIt.question: Our own retries turned a supplier's short outage into a long one. How do you handle it with the supplier and customers?
points: Own our part with the supplier.
Tell customers the truth about the delay.
Agree rate limits and a communication path with the supplier.
Consider a fallback supplier for critical flows.
Fund the resilience work.

tasks: How do you stop a storm in progress?
What do you put in place?

debrief.title: Stopping it
text: Stop or pause the consumers, let the provider recover, then resume gradually and watch error rates.

debrief.title: Putting in place
text: An inventory of retry policies across layers; a game day that simulates the provider failing.

sayIt.question: How would you stop a retry storm during an incident?
points: Recognise it: call volume far above normal, the dependency rate-limiting.
Stop the source: pause consumers or open the circuit.
Let the dependency recover, then resume slowly.
Map every retry layer afterwards.
Rehearse the failure.

tasks: Design the retry path for this consumer.
How does the consumer stay in its group while waiting?

debrief.title: The retry path
text: Remove retries from the gateway and HTTP client; keep one bounded retry with backoff and jitter in the payment service.
On repeated failure, publish the order to payments.retry.1m, then .10m, then .1h, then payments.dlq; a circuit breaker opens after a run of failures.

debrief.title: Staying in the group
text: When the circuit is open, call consumer.pause() on the partitions and keep calling poll, which returns nothing for paused partitions; resume() when it closes.

sayIt.question: How do you handle a downstream outage in a Kafka consumer?
points: Don't retry in place for long: it blocks the partition and breaks the poll interval.
Retry in one layer with exponential backoff and jitter, with a time limit.
Use delayed retry topics and a dead-letter topic, knowing it costs ordering.
Use a circuit breaker and pause the consumer while it is open.
Make the action idempotent, because retries repeat it.

scenario_levels.name: Running it
scenario_levels.about: What anyone accountable for a Kafka platform needs from operations: retention, schemas, monitoring and access.

scenarios.title: The disk full by morning
scenarios.outcome: A size limit set as if it were for the whole topic was per partition, and a broker's disk ran out of room overnight.

content.bookmark: retention.bytes is per partition, and retention removes whole segments. Multiply by partitions and replicas before you promise a disk budget.

check.prompt: A topic has 24 partitions and retention.bytes set to 50 GB. Roughly how much can one copy of the topic hold?
options: About 1.2 TB: the limit applies to each partition
check.why: retention.bytes is a per-partition limit. 24 × 50 GB is 1.2 TB for one copy, and each replica holds its own.

check.prompt: How does Kafka delete old data under the delete policy?
options: Record by record, as each expires
Only when a consumer has read it
A whole segment file at a time, once the segment qualifies
check.why: Retention and cleaning work a file at a time (segment.bytes defaults to 1 GiB), so usage moves in steps of a segment, not record by record.

check.prompt: What is the default time retention for a topic?
check.why: retention.ms defaults to 604800000, seven days, and records are not deleted when consumed.

check.prompt: A topic holds the latest price for each product, and old prices don't matter. Which cleanup policy fits?
options: compact: keep at least the latest value for each key
check.why: Compaction keeps the last known value per key, so the topic stays roughly the size of the product catalogue.

caseStudy.setting: A media company (fictional) streams video-player telemetry to player.events. The topic has 24 partitions and replication factor 3 on a 6-broker cluster, each broker with a 2 TB data disk. Finance asked the team to cap storage, and an engineer set retention.bytes=50000000000 (about 50 GB), meaning "50 GB for the topic".

events.when: Launch of a new series, Friday 20:00
events.what: Telemetry volume triples. The topic now fills far faster than the team's estimate.
A disk alert fires on one broker: 95% used. Two more brokers are above 85%. The on-call engineer doesn't know which topic is filling them.
The team finds player.events holding about 1.2 TB per copy, three copies across the cluster, with several other topics still to fit.

pipeline: Video players · send telemetry
player.events · 24 partitions, replication factor 3, retention.bytes 50 GB
Cluster · 6 brokers, 2 TB data disk each, 12 TB in total
Analytics consumers · read the last few hours
tasks: Why did a 50 GB cap not cap the topic at 50 GB?
What should the team have calculated?

debrief.title: Why the cap didn't cap
text: retention.bytes is per partition. 50 GB on each of 24 partitions allows 1.2 TB for one copy of the topic.
With replication factor 3, that is up to 3.6 TB across the cluster, about 30% of all its disk, for one topic.
Retention also removes whole segments, so usage drops in steps of a segment file, not smoothly.

debrief.title: The calculation that was missing
text: Disk for a topic = data rate × retention time × replication factor, or retention.bytes × partitions × replication factor, whichever is smaller.
Check it against free disk per broker, leaving room to re-copy a failed broker's data.
And ask what consumers need. Here they read only the last few hours, so a time limit (retention.ms of a day) fits better than a size limit.

debrief.title: Choosing the policy
text: Telemetry is a stream of independent events: delete policy, retention by time sized to how far back consumers must reread.
Latest-state data, like a price per product, suits compaction instead.

takeaway: retention.bytes is per partition, and every replica holds its own copy.
Disk = rate × time × replicas: work it out before launch.
Choose retention from how far back consumers must read.
content.honesty: If you haven't sized retention yourself, say so and walk through the arithmetic. If you have, lead with the numbers you used.

tasks: What questions would you ask about storage?
What would you specify?

debrief.title: Questions
text: "How far back does anyone need to reread this data?"
"What will this cost in disk at triple the volume?"

debrief.title: Specification
text: Retention is stated as a business need ("one day of telemetry"), with the disk it implies calculated and reviewed.

sayIt.question: How would you decide how long to keep event data?
points: Start from need: how far back must consumers reread or replay?
Add regulatory or audit needs.
Translate into disk: rate × time × replicas.
Check it at peak volume, not average.
Review when volumes change.

tasks: How do you answer Finance's cost question properly?

debrief.title: Cost
text: Give Finance the formula and the number: storage follows volume, retention and copies. A per-topic cap must be set per partition.

debrief.title: Before the next launch
text: Expected telemetry volume for launches goes into capacity planning, with storage and alerts checked.

sayIt.question: Finance asks you to cap data storage costs on a streaming platform. How do you respond?
points: Explain the drivers: volume, retention time, number of copies.
Agree retention from business need, not a round number.
Show the cost at peak and at growth.
Make sure the cap is set the way Kafka applies it, per partition.
Revisit at each big launch.

tasks: What do you do at 03:00?
What do you put in place after?

debrief.title: At 03:00
text: Find the biggest topics per broker, lower retention on player.events to what consumers need (for example retention.ms of a day), and watch segments being deleted.

debrief.title: After
text: Disk alerts at 70% with time to act; a per-topic storage review at creation.

sayIt.question: Brokers are running out of disk overnight. What do you do?
points: Find which topics are using the space.
Lower retention on the offending topic to what consumers need.
Confirm segments are being removed.
Add earlier alerts and a storage review per topic.
Review the sizing that let it happen.

tasks: What settings would you choose for player.events?
How would tiered storage change the picture?

debrief.title: Settings
text: cleanup.policy=delete, retention.ms of one day (86400000), retention.bytes left at -1 unless a hard guard is needed, and then set per partition.
Check: peak rate × 1 day × 3 replicas against free disk.

debrief.title: Tiered storage
text: Tiered storage moves completed segments to a remote store, keeping only recent data on broker disks. It needs a remote storage plugin, as Kafka ships none, and doesn't work with compacted topics.

sayIt.question: How do Kafka retention and compaction work, and how do you size storage?
points: Delete policy removes whole segments by time (default 7 days) or size.
retention.bytes is per partition.
Compaction keeps at least the latest value per key, with tombstones to delete.
Storage = rate × retention × replication factor, checked against free disk with headroom.
Tiered storage can move old segments off broker disks, with a plugin and limits.

scenarios.title: The field that broke the consumers
scenarios.outcome: A new required field, a compatibility check switched off to unblock a release, and every consumer that replayed history failed.

content.bookmark: Under BACKWARD compatibility, a new field needs a default so the new schema can still read old data. The compatibility check exists to refuse changes like this one.

check.prompt: In Avro, a reader's schema has a field the writer's data doesn't. What happens?
options: The reader's default is used; with no default, it is an error
check.why: Schema resolution fills a missing field from the reader's default. Without a default, reading fails.

check.prompt: What is Schema Registry's default compatibility mode?
check.why: BACKWARD: consumers using the new schema can read data written with the previous one.

check.prompt: Under BACKWARD compatibility, who upgrades first?
check.why: A BACKWARD-compatible schema can read old data, so consumers move to it first; producers follow.

check.prompt: In Protobuf, a field is removed. What should happen to its number?
options: Reuse it for the next new field
Mark it reserved and never reuse it
check.why: Protobuf identifies fields by number on the wire. Reusing a number makes old data decode into the wrong field.

caseStudy.setting: A travel company (fictional) publishes Booking events in Avro to bookings, with Schema Registry at its default BACKWARD compatibility. Several teams consume it; the analytics team regularly replays the whole topic to rebuild reports.

events.what: The bookings team adds a currency field with no default. The registry refuses the new schema as incompatible. Under release pressure, someone sets the subject's compatibility to NONE, and the schema is registered.
Consumers are upgraded to the new schema. Live data works. The analytics team's nightly replay from the start of the topic fails on the first old record.
Other teams that restart from older offsets fail the same way. Reports are a day late and the fix is disputed between teams.

pipeline: Bookings service · Avro serializer, schema version 7 adds currency (no default)
Schema Registry · subject bookings-value, compatibility switched from BACKWARD to NONE
bookings topic · 30 days of retention, old records written with version 6
Consumers · upgraded to version 7, some replay from the start
tasks: Why did reading old records fail?
What should the team have done when the registry refused the schema?

debrief.title: Why old records failed
text: Avro data carries no field names. The consumer reads each record with the writer's schema (version 6) and resolves it to its own (version 7).
Version 7 has currency; version 6 data doesn't. With no default to fill it in, resolution fails. Live records written with version 7 read fine, which is why the problem appeared only on replay.

debrief.title: What the refusal was telling them
text: BACKWARD compatibility means the new schema must read old data. The registry refused version 7 precisely because it couldn't. Switching to NONE removed the warning, not the problem.
The right change was to give currency a default (for example the company's base currency), which makes version 7 backward compatible.
BACKWARD is the default partly so consumers can rewind to the start of a topic, which is exactly what analytics does.

debrief.title: Guard rails
text: Only a schema owner can change a subject's compatibility, with review.
Check compatibility in the build, before deployment, so the failure is found by the team making the change.
Consider BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE, which checks against all earlier versions, not just the last.

takeaway: A new field needs a default to stay backward compatible.
The compatibility check refusing a schema is the system working.
Under BACKWARD, consumers upgrade first.
content.honesty: If you haven't managed schema evolution, say so and explain the modes and the upgrade order. If you have a story of a breaking change, lead with it.

tasks: What questions would you ask?

debrief.title: Questions
text: "Who reads this event, and does anyone replay old data?"
"Why was the compatibility check turned off, and who decided?"

debrief.title: Definition of done
text: A schema change passes the registry's compatibility check without changing the mode.
Consuming teams are told before the change, with the upgrade order.

sayIt.question: How would you manage a change to an event that several teams consume?
points: Treat the event as an interface with a contract.
Know who consumes it and how: live or replay.
Require the change to pass compatibility checks, not bypass them.
Plan the upgrade order with consumers.
Make bypassing the check a reviewed decision with an owner.

tasks: How do you handle the release-pressure decision?

debrief.title: Release pressure
text: The shortcut saved a day and cost several teams more. Make the cost of bypassing a safety check visible when the decision is made.

debrief.title: Users
text: Tell report users which reports are late and when they'll be right.

sayIt.question: A team bypassed a safety check to hit a release date and broke other teams. How do you respond?
points: Fix the impact first and communicate it.
Review the decision blamelessly: what pressure, what information.
Make bypassing checks an explicit, owned decision.
Plan for interface changes in the roadmap, not under pressure.
Agree how teams change shared events.

tasks: How do you resolve this now?
What process prevents it?

debrief.title: Now
text: Register a version 8 that gives currency a default, restore BACKWARD, move consumers to version 8, rerun the replay.

debrief.title: Process
text: Schema changes reviewed by consuming teams; compatibility-mode changes need a named approver.

sayIt.question: How would you coordinate a schema change across teams?
points: Identify every consumer.
Agree the compatibility mode and upgrade order.
Check compatibility in the build.
Communicate dates and roll out consumers first under BACKWARD.
Keep compatibility-mode changes under approval.

tasks: What schema change would you make?
How do you check compatibility automatically?

debrief.title: The change
text: Version 8: currency with a default value. Set the subject back to BACKWARD (or BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE).

debrief.title: Automatic checks
text: Test each schema change against the registry's compatibility check in CI, before deployment.
Restrict who can change a subject's compatibility setting.

sayIt.question: Explain schema compatibility modes and how you evolve an Avro schema safely.

FORWARD: old schema reads new data; producers first. FULL: both.
In Avro, add fields with defaults; a missing default breaks reading old data.
TRANSITIVE checks against all versions, not just the last.

scenarios.title: The alert nobody had
scenarios.outcome: Partitions ran on one copy for nine days without anyone knowing, until the last copy's broker failed.

content.bookmark: UnderReplicatedPartitions should be 0. A value above zero that lasts means the cluster is running with fewer copies than you think.

check.prompt: What is the normal value of the broker metric UnderReplicatedPartitions?
check.why: In a healthy cluster every partition has its full set of in-sync replicas. Non-zero means some followers have fallen out of the ISR.

check.prompt: How many brokers should report ActiveControllerCount = 1?
check.why: One active controller at a time. Zero or more than one is a problem to investigate.

check.prompt: Which two consumer signals do the Kafka docs say to watch?
options: Max lag below a threshold, and minimum fetch rate above zero
check.why: Lag shows falling behind; a fetch rate of zero shows a consumer that has stopped fetching altogether.

check.prompt: A topic has replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas 1 (the default). Two followers drop out of the ISR. Are acks=all writes accepted?
options: Yes, with only the leader holding them
check.why: acks=all waits for the current ISR, here just the leader, and min ISR 1 allows it. Writes succeed with one copy.

caseStudy.setting: An insurer (fictional) runs a 5-broker Kafka cluster for claims processing. Monitoring was set up quickly at launch: consumer lag dashboards and broker CPU. Topics use replication factor 3 and the default min.insync.replicas of 1.

events.what: A broker's network card starts dropping packets. Its followers can't keep up, and after replica.lag.time.max.ms the leaders remove it from the ISR of many partitions. A second broker is under maintenance and down.
Producers and consumers work normally. Lag is fine. Nobody looks at replication.
The broker leading many of those partitions fails. With no in-sync replica left, the partitions go offline. Claims processing stops.

pipeline: Claims producers · acks=all
Topics · replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas 1
Monitoring · consumer lag, broker CPU
Alerts · lag above threshold only
tasks: Which metric would have shown the problem on day 1?

debrief.title: The signal that was there
text: UnderReplicatedPartitions went above zero on day 1 and stayed there. IsrShrinksPerSec spiked too. Both are standard broker metrics with a normal value of 0.
Nobody alerted on them. Lag and CPU looked healthy, because producers and consumers were unaffected while one copy remained.

debrief.title: Why writes kept working
text: acks=all waits for the current in-sync replicas, not all assigned ones. With the ISR shrunk to the leader, acks=all was satisfied by one broker.
min.insync.replicas of 1 allowed it. At 2, writes would have been refused on day 1, which is disruptive but loud. UnderMinIsrPartitionCount would have shown it.

debrief.title: What happened on day 9
text: With every in-sync replica gone, Kafka by default waits for one to return rather than electing an out-of-sync replica (unclean.leader.election.enable=false). The partitions were unavailable rather than wrong.
The minimum alert set: UnderReplicatedPartitions > 0, UnderMinIsrPartitionCount > 0, ActiveControllerCount, UncleanLeaderElectionsPerSec, and consumer max lag and minimum fetch rate.

takeaway: Healthy clients can hide an unhealthy cluster.
Alert on under-replicated and under-min-ISR partitions, not just lag.
min ISR 2 turns silent risk into a loud error.

scenarios.title: Who deleted the topic?
scenarios.outcome: A clean-up script deleted a production topic, and the cluster's logs couldn't say who ran it.

content.bookmark: Without authentication and ACLs, anyone who can reach the brokers can do anything. And the default authorizer log records refusals, not successful actions.

check.prompt: With StandardAuthorizer, what happens to a resource that has no ACLs?
options: Only super users can, unless allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found=true
check.why: No ACLs means super users only. The allow.everyone setting reverses that and opens it to all, which is often switched on during setup and forgotten.

check.prompt: What does the shipped authorizer log record by default?
options: Denied requests at INFO; allowed ones only at DEBUG, which is off by default
check.why: The default log configuration routes the authorizer logger at INFO, so successful actions, like a delete, are not recorded.

check.prompt: An ALLOW ACL and a DENY ACL both match a request. What happens?
check.why: If any DENY ACL matches, the operation is denied regardless of ALLOW ACLs.

check.prompt: Can topics be deleted through the admin client by default?
options: No, deletion is off by default
check.why: Topic deletion is enabled by default, so who may delete is controlled by authorization.

caseStudy.setting: A healthcare scheduling company (fictional) runs Kafka for appointment events. During setup the cluster was given SASL/SCRAM authentication, but StandardAuthorizer was enabled with allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found=true "until ACLs are written". No ACLs were ever written. Developers have credentials for debugging.

events.what: A developer runs a script meant to delete test topics in a staging cluster. The script's config points at production. It deletes appointments.booked and three other topics.
Appointment booking fails. The topics are recreated empty within the hour, but their history is gone.
Compliance asks who deleted the topics and when. kafka-authorizer.log has no entry for the deletions. Nobody is sure which credentials were used.

Authorization · StandardAuthorizer, no ACLs, allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found=true

debrief.title: Why it was possible
text: Authentication worked: the cluster knew which user connected. Authorization didn't restrict anything, because with no ACLs and allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found=true, every authenticated principal could do every operation.
Topic deletion is on by default, so a delete from any principal succeeded.

debrief.title: Why there is no record
text: The authorizer logs denied requests at INFO and allowed ones only at DEBUG. With the shipped configuration, the file records refusals, not successful actions. The deletion was allowed, so it wasn't written.
For an audit trail of who changed what, enable allowed-request logging deliberately (at DEBUG, with the volume it brings) or require changes to go through a tool that records them.

debrief.title: Least privilege
text: Turn allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found off. Grant each service only what it needs, with prefixed ACLs per team namespace: producers WRITE and DESCRIBE, consumers READ on the topic and their group.
Give Delete, Alter and AlterConfigs on production topics only to a deployment principal used by reviewed automation, not to people.
Replication is not backup: the deletion removed every replica. Data that must survive this needs a copy outside the cluster.

takeaway: Authentication says who; ACLs say what they may do.
allow.everyone with no ACLs means everyone may do everything.
The default authorizer log shows refusals, not successes.

scenarios.title: The region that went dark
scenarios.outcome: A standby cluster existed, nobody had rehearsed using it, and a one-hour regional outage became five hours of downtime.

content.bookmark: Cross-cluster replication is asynchronous, so the recovery point is at least the replication lag. A failover that has never been rehearsed is a plan on paper only.

check.prompt: MirrorMaker 2 replicates the topic orders from a cluster aliased primary. What is it called on the standby, by default?
check.why: The default replication policy prefixes the source cluster's alias. Consumers failing over must read the renamed topic.

check.prompt: Besides topic data, what does MirrorMaker 2 replicate?
options: Topic configurations, consumer group offsets and ACLs
check.why: Replicated group offsets let a consumer group resume on the standby near where it stopped.

check.prompt: With asynchronous cross-cluster replication, what is the least data you can expect to lose in a sudden regional failure?
options: Whatever had not yet been replicated: the replication lag at that moment
check.why: Records are copied after they are written to the source, so the most recent ones may not have crossed. Measure the lag and state the RPO honestly.

check.prompt: Which tool keeps the same offsets on the destination as on the source?
options: Confluent Cluster Linking, a Confluent feature rather than part of Apache Kafka
check.why: Cluster Linking mirror topics are byte-for-byte copies with the same offsets. MirrorMaker 2 offsets on the target don't necessarily match the source.

caseStudy.setting: A payments processor (fictional) runs its primary Kafka cluster in one cloud region, with MirrorMaker 2 replicating to a standby cluster in another region. The disaster recovery plan says "fail over to the standby". It has never been tested end to end.

events.what: The primary region has a major network outage. Every service there is unreachable.

Nobody is sure who can declare a disaster. Producers' configs point at the primary's addresses. Consumers expect topic names without the primary. prefix. Credentials for the standby are missing for two services. Each fix is made by hand.
Payments resume on the standby. The primary region had recovered at 10:15. About 30 seconds of payments before the outage never reached the standby.

pipeline: Primary cluster · region A, all producers and consumers
MirrorMaker 2 · primary to standby, topics renamed primary.<name>
Standby cluster · region B, idle
DR plan · one line, never rehearsed
tasks: Why did failover take five hours when the outage lasted one?

debrief.title: Why it took so long
text: Every step of failover was being done for the first time: deciding, re-pointing producers, changing consumers to the prefixed topic names, finding credentials.
The standby had the data, but the systems around it weren't ready to use it. By the time they were, the primary was back, and failing back became a second problem.

debrief.title: What could be lost
text: MirrorMaker 2 copies records after they are written to the primary, so the last moments before an outage may never cross. Here, about 30 seconds.
That is the recovery point (RPO) this design really offers. It should be measured from the replication lag and agreed with the business, not discovered.

debrief.title: A plan worth having
text: Stated RPO and RTO per service. Who declares a disaster, and on what signals.
How producers find the standby; how each consumer group resumes, from replicated offsets and on prefixed names; what isn't replicated (schemas, connector configs, credentials).
How to fail back, and a scheduled rehearsal measured against the RPO and RTO.

takeaway: A standby you've never used is not a recovery plan.
Asynchronous replication means RPO is at least the lag.
Rehearse failover and failback, and measure them.

scenarios.title: The dashboard that counted twice
scenarios.outcome: A stream-processing instance restarted, some sales were counted twice, and late sales were dropped without a trace.

content.bookmark: Kafka Streams is at-least-once by default; exactly_once_v2 makes reading, updating state and writing results one transaction. Late records past a window's grace period are dropped.

check.prompt: What is Kafka Streams' default processing.guarantee?
check.why: The default is at_least_once. After a failure, some records can be processed again, so a count can go up twice.

check.prompt: What does exactly_once_v2 do?
options: Removes duplicates from the input topic
Commits the input offsets, state changes and output in one transaction, so a failure replays none of it twice
check.why: Within Kafka, the transactional producer writes output and consumer offsets atomically. It doesn't reach outside Kafka.

check.prompt: A sale arrives after its hourly window's grace period has passed. What happens?
options: It is added to the window
It goes into the next window
check.why: The grace period is how long a window waits for out-of-order records. After it, records for that window are dropped.

check.prompt: A downstream app reads the Streams output topic. What should it set to see only committed results?
check.why: read_committed hides records from aborted transactions, and those not yet committed.

caseStudy.setting: A retail chain (fictional) runs a Kafka Streams application that counts sales per store per hour from the sales topic and writes totals to sales.hourly. A dashboard used by store managers reads sales.hourly. The app runs three instances with default settings and an hourly window with a 5-minute grace period.

events.what: One instance is killed during a deployment. Its tasks move to the other instances, which restore state and continue from the last committed offsets.
Several stores' 11:00 totals on the dashboard are higher than their tills show.
Finance also finds sales from stores with poor connectivity missing entirely from Saturday's hourly totals. Those tills uploaded in batches up to 30 minutes late.

pipeline: Tills · send sales events, sometimes in late batches
sales topic · 12 partitions, so up to 12 tasks
Streams app · 3 instances, count per store per hour, grace 5 minutes, at_least_once
sales.hourly · read by the dashboard

debrief.title: Why totals were too high
text: With at_least_once, an instance that dies has processed records whose offsets weren't yet committed. The task restarts from the last commit and counts them again.
exactly_once_v2 commits offsets, state updates and output together. A restart then replays nothing that was already counted.

debrief.title: Why late sales vanished
text: Windows use event time. A sale from 11:40 belongs in the 11:00 window, whatever time it arrives.
With a 5-minute grace period, the 11:00 window stopped accepting records at about 12:05 of stream time. Sales uploaded later than that were dropped.
Set the grace period from how late data really arrives, here at least 30 minutes, and accept that totals for an hour change until it closes.

debrief.title: What readers must know
text: An aggregation's output is a table that updates: a later record revises the total. The dashboard should show the latest value per store and hour, not add them up.
Readers of the output should use read_committed once exactly_once_v2 is on.

takeaway: Streams defaults to at-least-once; counts need exactly_once_v2.
Records later than the grace period are dropped.
Windowed totals are updates; read the latest value.

scenarios.title: The sink that wrote twice
scenarios.outcome: A sink connector stopped on one bad record; the quick fix skipped 2,300 records silently and wrote thousands of others twice.

content.bookmark: A sink connector fails fast on a bad record by default. Tolerating errors needs a dead-letter topic, and a sink is at-least-once, so the target must be safe to write twice.

check.prompt: By default, what does a connector do when a record fails conversion or a transform?
options: Fails fast: errors.tolerance defaults to none, and the task stops
check.why: The defaults are errors.tolerance=none, errors.retry.timeout=0 and errors.log.enable=false: stop on the first error.

check.prompt: errors.tolerance=all is set with nothing else. What happens to bad records?
options: They go to a dead-letter topic
They are skipped, with no record kept unless logging or a dead-letter topic is configured
check.why: Tolerating errors only skips. errors.log.enable logs them; errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name sends them, for sink connectors, to a dead-letter topic.

check.prompt: A sink connector restarts after a crash. Where does it resume?
options: From its last committed offset, so records written after that commit are written again
Exactly after the last row written to the database
From the beginning of the topic
check.why: Connect manages offsets automatically, but a crash between writing and committing redelivers those records: at-least-once, Kafka's default.

check.prompt: Which mode should run production connectors?
options: Distributed: fault tolerant, scalable, managed through the REST API
check.why: Standalone is one process with no fault tolerance. Distributed workers share work and keep configs, offsets and status in Kafka topics.

caseStudy.setting: An energy company (fictional) streams smart-meter readings to meter.readings. A sink connector in a distributed Connect cluster writes them to an analytics database table, as plain inserts. Billing uses the table at month end.

events.what: A firmware bug makes some meters send readings with a malformed timestamp. The connector's task fails on the first one and stops. Lag grows all night.
To get data flowing, the on-call engineer sets errors.tolerance=all and restarts the connector. It catches up within the hour.
Billing finds about 2,300 readings missing with no trace of them anywhere, and thousands of readings in the table twice, from the hour before the failure.

pipeline: Smart meters · send readings to meter.readings
Connect · distributed, sink connector, tasks.max 6
Error handling · default (fail fast), then errors.tolerance=all
Analytics database · plain INSERT per reading

debrief.title: Where the readings went
text: errors.tolerance=all tells the connector to skip records that fail conversion or transforms. Without errors.log.enable or a dead-letter topic, skipping leaves no trace.
The readings are still in meter.readings until retention removes them, so they can be found and replayed if acted on in time.

debrief.title: Why others were written twice
text: The task had written records to the database after its last offset commit. On restart it resumed from the committed offset and wrote them again.
A sink is at-least-once unless the target cooperates. With plain inserts, every redelivery is a duplicate row. An upsert on a reading's natural key (meter ID and timestamp) makes a rewrite harmless.

debrief.title: The right configuration
text: errors.tolerance=all only together with errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name, errors.deadletterqueue.context.headers.enable=true and errors.log.enable=true.
An alert on records arriving in the dead-letter topic, with an owner who fixes and replays them.
Writes keyed so repeating them changes nothing.

takeaway: Fail-fast is the default; tolerance without a dead-letter topic is silent loss.
A sink is at-least-once; make the target safe to write twice.
A bad record is a signal, not just an obstacle.

debrief.title: Questions
text: "When a record can't be loaded, where does it go and who is told?"
"If a load repeats, do we get duplicates?"

debrief.title: Requirements
text: No reading is lost silently: every rejected reading is kept, alerted and owned.
Reloading the same readings never creates duplicates.

sayIt.question: What would you require of a pipeline that loads events into an analytics database?
points: No silent loss: rejected records kept and alerted.
No duplicates when loads repeat.
An owner for rejected records.
Reconciliation of counts against the source.
Tested failure handling before go-live.

tasks: What is the billing impact?
What do you tell customers?

debrief.title: Billing
text: Hold affected bills until readings are corrected: no bills from duplicated or missing readings.

debrief.title: Customers
text: If bills went out, correct them and explain; fix the firmware with the meter supplier.

sayIt.question: Data feeding customer bills was incomplete and duplicated. How do you handle it?
points: Stop wrong bills going out.
Correct the data from the source.
Tell affected customers.
Work with the supplier on the root cause.
Make data completeness a measured part of billing.

tasks: How do you recover the data?
What goes in the runbook?

debrief.title: Recovery
text: Remove duplicates by natural key, find the skipped readings in meter.readings before retention removes them, fix and reload them, reconcile counts.

debrief.title: Runbook
text: When a connector fails on bad data: enable the dead-letter topic, never tolerance alone; restart; review the dead-letter topic.

sayIt.question: A connector has stopped on bad data at night. What should on-call do?
points: Find the bad records from the task's error.
Restart with a dead-letter topic, not plain tolerance.
Confirm data flows and dead-letter alerts work.
Hand the rejected records to their owner.
Check for duplicates from the restart.

tasks: Write the connector's error settings.
How do you make the sink idempotent?

debrief.title: Error settings
text: errors.tolerance=all, errors.log.enable=true, errors.deadletterqueue.topic.name=meter.readings.dlq, errors.deadletterqueue.context.headers.enable=true.

debrief.title: Idempotent sink
text: Write with an upsert keyed on meter ID and reading timestamp, so a redelivered record overwrites itself. Or have the connector store offsets with the data in the same transaction, if it supports that.

sayIt.question: How do you run Kafka Connect reliably?
points: Distributed mode for fault tolerance, managed by REST.
Fail-fast by default; tolerance only with a dead-letter topic and logging.
Sinks are at-least-once; make writes idempotent.
Exactly-once for sources with exactly.once.source.support where the connector supports it.
Monitor task status, lag and the dead-letter topic.

scenarios.title: Sizing the platform
scenarios.outcome: Leadership asks how big a shared Kafka platform must be, and the first estimate forgot replication and the consumers.

content.bookmark: Disk = data per day × retention days × replication factor. Network out = data in × consumer groups, plus replication. Partitions come from measured throughput and needed parallelism, with headroom.

check.prompt: 0.5 TB of data a day, 7 days of retention, replication factor 3. How much disk does the data need across the cluster?
check.why: 0.5 × 7 = 3.5 TB for one copy, × 3 replicas = 10.5 TB, before headroom.

check.prompt: 20 MB/s is produced, with replication factor 3 and 4 consumer groups reading everything. Roughly how much leaves the brokers?
options: About 80 MB/s to consumers plus 40 MB/s of replication to followers
check.why: Each group reads the full 20 MB/s, and two followers each copy it once. Network often runs out before disk.

check.prompt: How many controllers do the KRaft docs typically recommend, and why?
options: 3 or 5: a majority must be alive, so 3 tolerate one failure and 5 tolerate two
check.why: The metadata quorum needs a majority. Combined broker-and-controller servers are not recommended for critical deployments.

check.prompt: Why decide partition counts up front, with headroom?
options: Consumers can't read more than 10 partitions
Partitions can't be reduced, and adding them later moves keys
check.why: Changing the count later is disruptive for ordered topics, and you can never go down.

caseStudy.setting: A bank (fictional) is consolidating five teams' event streams onto one shared Kafka platform. Leadership asks for a size and a cost. Inputs: peak 40 MB/s in, about 1 TB a day, 7 days of retention, replication factor 3, and each event read by 3 consumer groups on average.

events.what: A first estimate says 7 TB of disk and 3 brokers: 1 TB a day for 7 days.
Architecture review asks about replicas, consumer traffic, a broker failure and controllers. The estimate has none of them.
Leadership needs a defensible number by Friday, with the assumptions stated.

pipeline: 5 teams · producers, peak 40 MB/s in total
Topics · replication factor 3, min ISR 2, 7 days of retention
3 consumer groups per event on average
Cluster · brokers and KRaft controllers to be sized
tasks: What did the first estimate leave out?
Work out disk, network and the shape of the cluster.

debrief.title: What was missing
text: Replication: every byte is stored three times. 1 TB × 7 days × 3 = 21 TB, not 7.
Headroom: room to grow, and to re-copy a failed broker's data onto the others. Keeping disks around half full, a common planning choice rather than a Kafka rule, means about 42 TB of raw disk.
Consumers and replication on the network: at peak 40 MB/s in, 80 MB/s of follower replication, and 120 MB/s to three consumer groups.

debrief.title: The shape of the cluster
text: Brokers: divide disk and network by what one broker can carry on your hardware, keep at least 3 for replication factor 3, and add one so the cluster still holds the load with a broker down.
Controllers: 3 dedicated KRaft controllers, so the metadata quorum survives one failure. Combined servers suit development, not critical systems.
Partitions per topic: from measured per-partition throughput and needed consumer parallelism, the larger, with headroom.

debrief.title: What to measure before committing
text: Per-partition throughput with real record sizes and compression; consumer processing rates; recovery time after a broker loss.
If retention is the main driver of disk, tiered storage can move older segments off broker disks, with a remote storage plugin and its limits.

takeaway: Disk is data × retention × replicas, plus headroom.
Network out is consumers plus replication, and often the real limit.
State the assumptions, measure, and plan for losing a broker.
content.honesty: If you haven't sized a cluster, say so and do the arithmetic out loud with stated assumptions. If you have, lead with the number that turned out wrong.

tasks: What inputs would you get from the five teams?
What would you include in the platform's service level?

debrief.title: Inputs
text: Peak and average volume, record size, retention need, how many consumers, and growth over two years, per team.

debrief.title: Service level
text: Durability (replication factor 3, min ISR 2), availability with one broker down, and lag targets per consumer.

sayIt.question: How would you gather requirements for a shared streaming platform?
points: Volumes at peak and average, record sizes, growth.
Retention needs from each team's replay requirements.
Number of consumers per stream.
Durability and availability expectations.
Owners and change process per team.

tasks: How do you present the number to leadership?
How do you allocate cost across teams?

debrief.title: Presenting
text: Show the formula, the assumptions and a range, and what would change it: retention, consumers, growth.

debrief.title: Allocating cost
text: By each team's bytes in × retention × replicas, plus consumer traffic, so teams see the cost of their choices.

sayIt.question: How would you justify the size and cost of a shared Kafka platform?
points: Show the drivers: volume, retention, replication, consumers.
State assumptions and give a range.
Include headroom for failure and growth.
Allocate cost by usage so choices have visible cost.
Revisit with real measurements.

tasks: How do you plan the rollout?
What capacity process do you set up?

debrief.title: Rollout
text: Onboard one team at a time, measuring real throughput and lag before the next.

debrief.title: Capacity process
text: Quarterly capacity review against disk, network and partition counts; onboarding requests include volumes and retention.

sayIt.question: How would you roll out a shared platform to several teams?
points: Onboard in stages, measuring as you go.
Require volumes and retention with each request.
Review capacity regularly.
Keep headroom for a broker loss.
Communicate limits and costs.

tasks: Do the arithmetic.
What would you benchmark?

debrief.title: Arithmetic
text: Disk: 1 TB/day × 7 × 3 = 21 TB, about 42 TB raw at half full.
Network at peak: 40 in, 80 replication, 120 out, so about 200 MB/s leaving brokers in total.

debrief.title: Benchmarks
text: kafka-producer-perf-test and kafka-consumer-perf-test with real record sizes, acks=all and compression on, on the target hardware; then a broker-loss test while loaded.

sayIt.question: Walk me through sizing a Kafka cluster.
points: Disk: data per day × retention × replication factor, plus headroom.
Network: in, plus replication, plus each consumer group.
Partitions: the larger of throughput need and parallelism need, with headroom.
Brokers: enough for disk and network, at least 3, plus one spare; 3 or 5 KRaft controllers.
Measure on real hardware and test a broker loss.

diagnostic_questions.question: How is Kafka different from a traditional message queue, and when would you not use it?
points: Kafka keeps events in a retained, append-only log; reading does not delete them.
Each consumer group keeps its own offsets, so many applications read the same topic independently and can replay.
Inside one group, partitions are shared out among consumers for parallel work.
Ordering is per partition, not across a whole topic.
Not the right tool for synchronous request-response, or a small queue needing per-message routing and acknowledgement.

diagnostic_questions.question: A topic has 12 partitions. How do you keep each order's events in sequence, and what happens if one customer sends most of the traffic?
points: Records with the same key go to the same partition, where order is preserved.
Key by the smallest entity that must be ordered, such as the order id.
A dominant key makes one hot partition; adding partitions does not split one key.
Remedies: bucket the key, relax ordering where allowed, isolate the tenant, or aggregate, each giving something up.
Adding partitions later remaps keys and briefly breaks per-key order.

diagnostic_questions.question: Which settings make sure an acknowledged write survives a broker failure, and what do you trade for it?
points: Replication factor 3 so each partition has copies on three brokers.
acks=all, so the leader waits for every in-sync replica.
min.insync.replicas=2, so writes are refused instead of acknowledged on a single copy.
Unclean leader election off, so an out-of-sync replica never becomes leader.
The trade: some write availability when brokers are down, and a little latency.

diagnostic_questions.question: How would you make sure a payment event is not lost and not applied twice?
points: At-least-once by default: producer retries, consumer commits after processing.
The idempotent producer removes retry duplicates within a producer session.
Transactions plus read_committed give exactly-once only between Kafka topics.
For the payment system itself, an idempotency key so a repeated event is harmless.
Commit before processing loses records on a crash; commit after processing repeats them.

diagnostic_questions.question: A consumer group is falling behind. How do you find out why, and what do you do?
points: Measure lag per partition: log-end offset minus committed offset, with kafka-consumer-groups.
Lag on one partition suggests a hot key or a poison record; on all, slow processing or too few consumers.
Check what consumers wait on (database, API) before scaling them.
More consumers help only up to the partition count.
Watch for rebalance storms: processing longer than max.poll.interval.ms.

diagnostic_questions.question: The downstream payment API is down for an hour. How should your Kafka consumer behave?
points: Separate poison records (dead-letter topic) from transient failures (retry).
Bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter, and a timeout on every call.
A circuit breaker so the consumer stops calling a dependency that is down.
Retry topics for waits longer than a poll interval, accepting the loss of per-key order.
Kafka buffers the backlog only within retention; watch lag and degrade gracefully.

diagnostic_questions.question: How do you let a producer team change an event's schema without breaking consumers?
points: Use Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema with a schema registry; records carry a schema ID.
The registry checks each new version against the subject's compatibility mode.
BACKWARD (the default): add fields with defaults; upgrade consumers first.
Protobuf: never change or reuse field numbers; reserve deleted ones.
A registry checks registrations, not every record, so restrict who writes.

diagnostic_questions.question: How would a Kafka-based platform survive the loss of a whole region?
points: In-cluster replication across zones covers brokers and zones, not the cluster or region.
A second cluster, replicated with MirrorMaker 2 or Confluent Cluster Linking.
Cross-cluster replication is asynchronous, so the RPO is the replication lag.
Active-passive for strict consistency; active-active needs conflict rules.
A rehearsed failover for producers and consumers, and backups outside Kafka for data that can't be regenerated.
